This talk is about one question: given a state of two quantum systems, is it separable or entangled? I will compare tests that only use information an experiment can access, a few numbers called moments, rather than the full state. Joint work with Cécilia Lancien; the paper is peer reviewed and will appear in Letters in Mathematical Physics.

Same matrix entries, two rearrangements: the partial transpose exchanges j and l, realignment exchanges j and k. Realignment gives another test, the trace norm of rho^R is at most 1 for separable states (Chen and Wu 2003; Rudolph 2003). It can detect some PPT entangled states. We will meet it again on the comparison slide.

Level d squared minus one is exact, and no lower level is: a state whose partial transpose has one tiny negative eigenvalue and d squared minus one distinct positive ones passes level d squared minus two. Finite collapse is not automatic for hierarchies of relaxations: the symmetric extension hierarchy is never exact at a finite level once d is at least three (Fawzi, Commun. Math. Phys. 2021). If asked: the first d squared moments already fix the spectrum of rho^Gamma (Newton identities), and the sign conditions of Neven et al. (npj Quantum Inf. 2021) decide PPT from them. The Hankel tests are linear matrix inequalities that never use the dimension, which is why they need more moments.

Slightly more mixed than uniform, a typical state passes the three-moment test; slightly less mixed, it is detected. The theorem says nothing at lambda exactly equal to 1; our simulations at s equal to d squared detect about one state in five.

This is the main result in one picture. Each bar shows how far a test typically detects entanglement. At 1.5 d squared, three moments miss the entanglement while five moments detect it. Even three moments go further than realignment, which stops near 0.72 d squared: realignment does poorly here. Like PPT, realignment needs the full spectrum of a rearranged state, the singular values of rho^R, whereas the three-moment test uses two numbers, p2 and p3. But this is typical behaviour in this model, not a ranking of the tests on every state: realignment can even detect some PPT entangled states, which no test of this hierarchy can. Beyond 4 d squared none of these tests detects anything, yet the states stay entangled up to s of order d cubed. All these tests live at the scale d squared; separability lives at the scale d cubed, up to log factors.
